newsitem.title: Sweden: FOCUS-H&M figures amaze, but share seen too dear.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-H&M figures amaze, but share seen too dear.

text.p: Swedish fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz amazed analysts with its six-month earnings report which outshone expectations, but several still said the share was expensive.
"Pre-tax profit was about 20 percent higher than expected but the share is very expensive," Christian Diebitsch, analyst at Paribas in London, told Reuters.

"It is trading at 35 times the expected profit in 1997, 30 times the expected 1998 profit and 26 times the 1999 profit. It's the most expensive retail stock in Europe and the most expensive stock in Sweden by 1997-1999 profit expectations."
Diebitsch said Paribas was considering downgrading the share to "sell" from "hold" because of its very high valuation.
H&M said pre-tax profit surged 63 percent to 1.01 billion crowns ($130.1 million) in the first half of its 1996/1997 fiscal year while analysts in a Reuter poll targeted 832 million crowns.

Shares rocketed 26 crowns to an all-time intra-day high of 293 on the Stockholm Stock Exchange just after the report but slipped back somewhat to trade at 285 crowns at 1415 GMT, up 18 crowns or seven percent.
Operating profit after depreciation rose to 1.01 billion crowns from 646 million, while earnings per share jumped to 3.16 crowns from 1.94 and gross margin advanced to 13.5 percent from 11.7 percent.
"You have to say that gross margins are fantastic," said Anna-Karin Olsson, analyst at Den Norske Bank.
Profit was boosted by a 31 percent sales increase to 10.18 billion crowns as the group took relatively large market shares on all markets, bucking sluggish European market trends.
"Despite the weak (important) German market H&M succeeds in presenting such a strong report," said Mats Liss, analyst at Swedbank. "When the market turns up, the group will be well positioned there."
H&M chief executive expected economic trends to strengthen.
"I'm somewhat optimistic," CEO and main owner Stefan Persson told Reuters. "I think I can spot some upturns, even if some markets look sluggish."

The growth potential is significant on most markets, including Germany where H&M has a market share of one percent, Persson said. The more mature markets in Sweden, Norway and Denmark are exceptions, he said.

Analysts who said they would upgrade full-year profit estimates were astonished to see the mark's weakening against the dollar did not sting H&M more as it did, considering the amount of H&M's purchasing and sales in marks.
"It's surprising that the dollar doesn't have more of an impact," Olsson said. "The group has an incredibly slim purchasing side and this is really good, but the share isn't cheap."

But the share could be buoyed in the short-term as Persson will meet international investors in London and New York this week to explain why the company moved from the Stockholm Stock Exchange's main A list to its smaller O list, analysts said.

A 1996 law forces Swedes with wealth exceeding 900,000 crowns to pay 1.5 percent tax on 100 percent of the value of shares listed on the A list, up from 75 percent, while shares on the smaller O list remain exempt from tax.
The tax hit Persson and his family, who hold 38.4 percent of H&M's capital.
Analysts noted that H&M kept expanding at roughly the expected rate, opening 21 new stores in the six-month period ending on May 31 and planning to set up about 35 stores in the autumn of 1997.

In Finland, where H&M plans to open five stores this autumn, Persson said he expected to take as large a market share as H&M holds in Sweden, which would mean 13-14 percent. ($ = 7.763 Swedish Crowns)
